name: Retrograde femoral nailing through the intercondylar notch
corridor: Small infrapatellar medial-paratendinous or transpatellar route to an intercondylar start aligned with Blumensaat line

positioning.text: Position supine with the knee flexed about 30 degrees over a radiolucent support, allowing true AP and lateral imaging from the notch through the fracture.

setup.text: Prep the full limb, assess knee contamination and prior implants, plan reduction, and verify that the intercondylar notch and Blumensaat line are visible.

surface_landmarks.text: Mark patellar borders, inferior pole, patellar tendon, tibial plateau, joint line, femoral axis, and fluoroscopic Blumensaat line.

incision.text: Make an approximately 2-cm longitudinal midline incision just distal to the inferior patellar pole over the patellar tendon.

superficial_interval.text: Spread medial parapatellar tissues longitudinally and gently retract the patellar tendon laterally, or use a controlled tendon split when indicated.

deep_interval.text: Enter the intercondylar notch at the canal axis: centered on AP and in line with Blumensaat line laterally, anterior and lateral to the PCL femoral attachment.

layers.text: Skin, infrapatellar soft tissue, medial paratendinous interval or tendon split, joint capsule and synovium, intercondylar cartilage entry, then distal femoral canal.

structures_encountered.text: Patellar tendon, infrapatellar fat and synovium, trochlear/intercondylar cartilage, ACL and PCL attachment regions, notch, and distal femoral canal are encountered.

structures_at_risk.text: ACL, PCL attachment, weight-bearing cartilage, patellar tendon, tibial plateau, and popliteal neurovascular structures are at risk.

danger_zones.text: A start posterior to Blumensaat line threatens the ACL, an anterior or off-center start injures cartilage or drives malalignment, and uncontrolled posterior plunging threatens the popliteal bundle.

retraction_hazards.text: Retract the patellar tendon gently and avoid levering sleeves against cartilage; adjust knee flexion rather than forcing the guidewire past patella or tibial plateau.

exposure.text: Provides direct access from the intercondylar notch into the distal femoral canal with minimal fracture-site dissection.

limitations.text: The approach violates the knee joint and may contribute to anterior knee pain; the wide metaphyseal canal can permit varus-valgus or sagittal malalignment.

extensions.text: Enlarge the parapatellar interval for direct notch visualization or add limited fracture reduction and blocking techniques when metaphyseal alignment cannot be controlled.

indications.text: Use for selected distal femoral and shaft fractures, including compatible periprosthetic patterns, when sufficient distal bone and an accessible intercondylar box permit stable fixation.

relative_contraindications.text: Avoid with active knee sepsis, incompatible femoral components or closed box, inadequate distal segment, open contaminated knee injury, or articular anatomy preventing a safe start.

implant_implications.text: Select nail length and distal fixation for the fracture and any arthroplasty stem, countersink the nail beneath cartilage, and use blocking strategies when the metaphyseal canal does not guide alignment.

fluoroscopy_implications.text: Every start-point step requires AP and lateral fluoroscopy; verify central notch entry, Blumensaat alignment, fracture length and axes, nail depth, and locking-screw safety.

closure.text: Irrigate the knee thoroughly to remove drilling debris, repair tendon or paratendinous tissues and capsule, and close skin in layers.

complications.text: Complications include ACL or cartilage injury, knee pain and stiffness, septic arthritis, patellar-tendon injury, malalignment, popliteal injury, nonunion, and hardware prominence.

bailouts.text: If the start cannot be proven safe or the distal segment cannot be aligned, stop reaming, improve direct visualization and reduction, add blocking fixation, or convert to plating.

procedure_applications.condition: A distal femoral or selected shaft fracture is suitable for retrograde fixation and the knee and implant environment permit intercondylar entry

questions.question: Where is the retrograde start on the lateral view?
questions.answer: In line with Blumensaat line, not posterior to it.

questions.question: Where is it relative to the PCL attachment?
questions.answer: Anterior and lateral to the proximal PCL attachment.

questions.question: Why is about 30 degrees of knee flexion used?
questions.answer: Less flexion lets the tibial plateau obstruct entry; greater flexion brings the patella and articular surface into danger.
